summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and, in 2020, became the first Central American country to adopt marriage equality. The ILGA World database records the resulting LGBTI legal framework. For a trans visitor this is the most permissive legal setting in the region.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. The electoral authority processes name changes on official identification through a simple, free procedure; before 2018 a judicial order was required for a name change. A 2016 bill to permit change of name and gender without surgery or judicial permission was unsuccessful.

The Penal Code was strengthened in 2020. Article 112 provides 20 to 35 years' imprisonment for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation, article 380 one to three years for exclusion or segregation on that basis, and article 386bis three to ten years for inflicting physical or mental pain, intimidation, coercion or blackmail.

No visa or entry policy targeting LGBTQ travellers appears in current law. In December 2018 the president signed executive decrees covering immigration rights for binational same-sex couples. One historical episode sits in the record: in 1990 the Interior Ministry instructed Costa Rican consulates not to grant visas to women travelling unaccompanied by men, in an attempt to block foreign lesbians from attending an international meeting. The instruction is decades old and is not described as current.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care. The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and specific protective legislation while recording her concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups. She recommended intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

Placement of trans prisoners is governed by an official policy. The Justice Ministry announced in June 2017 that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual may choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, strictly voluntary and decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners, and Spain's system was cited as the model. Implementation did not match the policy. In June 2019 a trans woman was held at the CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility, where she had transitioned while incarcerated; the Justice Ministry told reporters there were 23 transgender people in the national system at the time. She recounted identity-targeted abuse, including a rape with a broomstick handle at La Reforma in Alajuela witnessed by a custodian. The Supreme Court ruled in 2011 that same-sex couples have equal access to conjugal visits in prison.

Official recognition is real and contested. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia in 2008, with the president and health minister directing public institutions to support activities for the eradication of homophobia; the day was designated a national day by executive order the same year. The rainbow flag flew at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag in May 2014, prompting lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties to call it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending. In June 2019 the president became the first Costa Rican head of state to march at the San José pride parade, which drew about 100,000 participants, and in 2018 he issued a public apology for past state-promoted persecution, raids, arbitrary arrests and beatings. Rollback pressure runs alongside this: a conversion-therapy bill has been stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
tangentialFactors:
Queer and trans policy in Costa Rica is a live electoral fault line rather than settled ground. The 2018 general election was sharply divisive over same-sex marriage, and a 2012 poll found 60% of 18 to 34-year-olds supporting equal rights for same-sex couples. Conservative legislators organised openly against official recognition in 2014, and the stalled conversion-therapy bill shows the legislative ceiling on further protections.

Religious opposition shapes the environment beyond the statutes. Comprehensive sex education campaigns are described as almost nonexistent in public high schools because of Catholic Church and other religious-group pressure, a factor that bears on the health information a visitor or resident can expect to encounter.

Police conduct has shifted over time. Harassment and raids of LGBTQ people and private establishments were formerly commonplace while homosexuality was technically legal; the 2000 Supreme Court ruling ordering a gay sauna to remain open held that subjective criteria of morality and proper behaviour have no legal basis. The same 2000 jurisprudence found in vitro fertilisation unconstitutional, a limit on assisted reproduction that applies to couples generally.

The constitutional framework also constrains institutional discrimination: in 1993 the Ministry of Education advised that a university's policy of expelling LGBTQ students and firing LGBTQ staff would likely violate articles 20, 33 and 70 if enforced.

Costa Rica's trajectory is an outlier in Central America on decriminalisation, marriage equality and administrative gender recognition, but it shares the region's pattern of conservative legislative resistance and of protection resting on executive and judicial action rather than durable statutory consensus.
localsOnly:
Survivor's pension coverage was extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans, announced by the Ministry of Labor on 25 June 2016, with an individual survivor benefit approved on 29 June 2018. The teachers' separate budget was excluded from that extension, leaving an unresolved gap for that scheme.

Gender marker and name changes on Costa Rican identity documents are handled as a free administrative procedure by the electoral authority, without surgery or a judicial order. Residents also retain the judicial route for name changes that has been available since 2013.

Prison policy for trans inmates is a documented, voluntary choice of facility decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, supported by a circular ordering a census of self-identified trans prisoners. The 2019 reporting indicates the policy was not consistently applied and that trans women remained housed with men, in some cases facing abuse in front of custodial staff.

The 2018 apology for state persecution and the executive decrees on immigration rights for binational same-sex couples are instruments available to residents and their foreign partners, alongside the survivor-pension entitlement.

Hostile institutional practices have a documented history: the 1993 university expulsions and dismissals, the 1990 consular visa instruction targeting unaccompanied women, and formerly routine police raids on private establishments.
outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement of the 2020 hate-crime provisions is not evidenced in the inventory. The inventory supplies the penalties and article numbers but no conviction data, case outcomes or prosecutorial practice, so the practical reliability of those sentences for a trans complainant is unresolved.

Whether the June 2017 Justice Ministry circular and the ordered census of self-identified trans prisoners remain in force, and whether a dedicated trans module was ever established, is unresolved; the 2019 reporting describes the placement choice as available but documents a trans woman held in a men's facility.

The scope of the 2025 reversals is not fully sourced. The inventory records the scrapping of the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol but does not establish whether gender-affirming care funding or the 2018 gender-marker decree were affected; no such effect is reported.

The status of the conversion-therapy bill after its 2019 committee report is unresolved beyond the inventory's description of it as stalled.

The current status of the 1990 consular visa instruction is not directly sourced; the inventory describes it as a decades-old measure and does not characterise it as current, but no formal withdrawal is documented.

The survivor-pension exclusion for the teachers' budget and the 2000 in vitro fertilisation ruling are recorded in a legal reference without detail on later amendments; whether either position has since changed is not sourced here.
